$comment: Maestro's own MCP tool surface, served by `maestro-server mcp` (see mcp_stdio.rs). Descriptions are the ONLY documentation the agent receives, so prose here is behaviour, not commentary. Adding a tool here also needs an arm in the host's `host_tools::handle`, or the gateway will forward calls nobody answers.

tools.name: canvas_create
tools.description:
Open a canvas surface in Maestro's side panel. A surface is an HTML document you write — HTML, CSS and JavaScript — rendered in a sandboxed frame beside the conversation. Always the first call for a new surfaceId, before canvas_data or canvas_update. Reuse one surfaceId for a whole answer; a new surface per tool call produces disconnected panels. Never narrate these calls to the user — they see the rendered surface, not the machinery.

WRITING THE DOCUMENT
- Give every meaningful element an `id`. Controls with an id answer canvas_await, and elements with an id are the ones the user can annotate and point you at.
- theme `maestro` (the default) gives you Tailwind compiled in the frame with Maestro's own tokens: `bg-card`, `text-muted-foreground`, `border-border`, `rounded-lg`, `bg-primary`, `text-destructive`, `bg-chart-1`. Writing shadcn-flavoured Tailwind produces a surface that looks like the rest of the app — `<div class='rounded-lg border bg-card p-4 shadow-sm'>` is a Maestro card.
- theme `tailwind` is Tailwind with its own stock tokens, for mocking up a project that uses Tailwind. theme `none` injects nothing, for a mockup carrying the target project's own CSS.
- Assets are `https:` URLs or `data:` URIs. Relative paths and `file://` do NOT resolve — the frame has no base URL and no access to the disk. Icons are inline `<svg>`, not image files.
- Charts: inline `<svg>` for bars, lines and sparklines, which always works. For real axes, scales and tooltips add a CDN library — and guard it, because the user may be offline:
  `<script src='https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/uplot@1.6.32/dist/uPlot.iife.min.js' onerror="document.getElementById('chart').textContent='Chart library unavailable offline'"></script>`
- `window.maestro` is available in the frame: `maestro.emit(id, kind, value)` answers a pending canvas_await from your own code, `maestro.record(id, value)` notes a value without answering, `maestro.onData(cb)` reads what canvas_data pushed, and `maestro.fetch(url, init)` performs a request from the host machine against the origins you declared in `sources`.
- A control your own script handles should either call `preventDefault()` or carry `data-maestro-ignore`. Otherwise Maestro also reports the click, and a button that only redraws something in the frame consumes the canvas_await you were holding for a real answer.
- Anything the frame fails to load or run — a blocked asset, an offline CDN, a thrown exception — comes back to you on the result of your next canvas call on this surface.

surfaceId.description: Your identifier for this surface; reuse it in every later call.

html.description: The document. A full `<html>` page or a fragment — Maestro prepends its own head either way.

theme.description: `maestro` for anything that should look like the app. `none` for a mockup of someone else's product.

sources.description: Origins `maestro.fetch` may reach, e.g. ["https://api.example.com"]. Anything else is refused. The user is shown this list. Secrets in request headers end up in the transcript and in the saved file.

tools.name: canvas_update
tools.description:
Change a surface. With `target`, the element with that id is replaced in the live frame: no reload, so scroll position, focus, canvas bitmaps and anything the user typed survive — prefer this for content. Without `target`, the whole document is replaced and the frame reloads, losing all of that and re-running your script from the top.

The replacement is assigned as `outerHTML`, so the element itself is a new node: listeners your script bound to it are gone, and a `<script>` inside the replacement never runs. A control your own JavaScript drives has to be rewired, which means a document-level listener that survives the swap — or a full replace. Static content, rows, values and labels are what `target` is for.

Element ids are scoped to their surface, so two forms may both use `branch` without colliding. Neither `title` nor `sources` can be changed after canvas_create.

html.description: With `target`, the replacement for that element — include the element itself, with its id, or you lose the anchor. Without `target`, the whole document.

target.description: Id of the element to replace. Omit to replace the document.

tools.name: canvas_data
tools.description:
Store data on a surface at a JSON Pointer path. The document subscribes with `maestro.onData(function (data) { ... })`, reading `data['/rows']`. Use it for values that change while the surface stays the same — a table's rows, a chart's series — so a refresh is one small call instead of a document rewrite.

Subscribe; do not read `maestro.data` while your script is initialising. It is empty then — the bag arrives just after the document loads, and `onData` fires at that moment with everything in it.

The bag outlives the document. A full canvas_update reloads the frame, and `onData` then delivers every value you have ever pushed as though it were new — so a handler that acts on what it receives (appending a row, playing a move) must be able to tell a replay from a change. Push a counter alongside the value and ignore anything not newer than what the document has already seen.

tools.name: canvas_await
tools.description: Wait for the user to act on a surface's controls, and return what they did. This is what makes the controls answer — render the form with canvas_create or canvas_update first, then call this. Returns `{event:{surfaceId,componentId,kind,value,values}}`, where `componentId` is the element's `id` and `values` holds every field on that surface, so one form is one round trip. A `button[id]` click, a `form[id]` submit, and any `maestro.emit` call all answer it; inputs with an `id` or `name` fill `values` without answering. Omit `surfaceId` to take whichever canvas the user acts on: they can page between every surface you have drawn, and the event names the one they used. Pass `surfaceId` only to insist on a particular canvas — one that does not match a canvas you created waits for nothing. Returns `{timeout:true}` if nothing happened in the window; call again to keep waiting. Keep an open wait for as long as the surface is worth interacting with, re-arming after every event and every timeout: while one is open the user's actions reach you directly, and while none is open each one costs a whole turn. Nothing is lost either way — an action with no wait open is held and delivered to the next wait you arm, or as a prompt once you go idle — but a held action is one the user is waiting on, so arm the next wait before doing anything else. A surface only the user's own script reacts to — a filter that redraws a chart in the frame — never answers a wait and does not need one. Stop re-arming when the exchange is finished; the user can always type, which ends the wait.

surfaceId.description: Restrict the wait to one surface. Omit to accept any.

tools.name: create_task
tools.description: Create a Maestro task in the Planning column of the current project. Use when the user asks for work to be tracked, or when you find follow-up work worth recording. The task is created immediately — say what you created and quote the id.

description.description: Markdown. What needs doing and why.

tools.name: get_task
tools.description: Read a Maestro task: its description, status, labels, and the outcome thread of what previous sessions concluded about it. Omit `id` for the task this session was started for — the prompt you were given is a paraphrase of a card, and the card is where the user put the detail, the acceptance criteria and the history. Read it before assuming what the work is. The thread carries the last 20 entries, newest kept.

id.description: Omit for the task this session is working on.

tools.name: update_task
tools.description:
Change a Maestro task. Only the fields you pass are touched; omit `id` for the task this session is working on.

Moving `status` is the same move as the user dragging the card, so make it when the work has actually reached that state — `Review` when you are finished and want it looked at, not when you expect to be finished. The user is watching the board, so a wrong move is visible and misleading rather than harmless.

id.description: Omit for the task this session is working on.

labels.description: Replaces the whole list, so include the ones you are keeping.

tools.name: comment_task
tools.description: Add a note to a task's outcome thread: what you concluded, what you tried that did not work, what the next session needs to know. This transcript is discarded when the session closes and the thread is not, so anything worth keeping belongs here rather than only in your reply. Omit `id` for the task this session is working on.

id.description: Omit for the task this session is working on.

tools.name: list_tasks
tools.description: List the current project's tasks, newest first. Archived tasks are excluded. Use it to check whether work is already tracked before creating a task.
